progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b10 (route level only, being designed in parallel: "Define cases, population and time window" and "Calculate and compare rates without mixing denominators"): a rate is cases out of a population over a time; incidence counts new cases, prevalence existing cases, mortality deaths. From b07: carcinogens in smoke reach airway cells and damage DNA; dose and pack-years; latency; men's lung cancer rates in Australia fell from the early 1980s, decades after smoking fell (b07 attempt 1). From Year 11 Working Scientifically: variables, controls, validity, reliability. Not assumed: observational study, intervention study, randomised controlled trial, case-control study, control (as a matched patient), bias, confounder, cohort study, dose-response, benefit (as an evaluate term).
progression.startsWith: Between 1922 and 1947, lung cancer deaths in England and Wales rose about fifteen times. Smoking had grown, but so had tarred roads, car exhaust and factory smoke. In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published the first of their studies on smoking. So how do we judge an epidemiological study, and what it achieved?
progression.stopsAfter: distinguishing observational from intervention studies and explaining why randomisation helps balance other differences by chance, and why smoking could not be randomised; describing the 1950 case-control study (lung cancer patients matched with controls, smoking histories compared) and evaluating it (quick, matched for age and sex; smoking recalled, so open to recall bias; strong association, not proof of cause); explaining a confounder; describing the British Doctors cohort (questionnaires in 1951, deaths recorded forward in time) and evaluating it (exposure recorded before the later deaths, large and long; doctors not typical, self-reported, still observational; the strongest ethical design); explaining how strength, dose-response, timing, consistency, mechanism and the effect of quitting together support a causal conclusion; evaluating the benefit as a chain from finding to checked outcome, with Australia's tobacco control, and its limits (delay, unequal reach, costs to participants); applying the frame to an unseen case-control study and the chain to the folate studies.

teaching.task: Between 1922 and 1947, lung cancer deaths in England and Wales rose about fifteenfold. How do we judge an epidemiological study, and what it achieved?
teaching.causalExplanation: Earlier, you measured disease with rates. Now we judge the studies behind them. An observational study watches what people already do, such as smoking, and compares their disease rates. In an intervention study, researchers decide who gets an exposure. In a randomised controlled trial, chance decides the groups, which helps balance other differences. But nobody could ethically make people smoke for decades, so the smoking evidence had to be observational. Their first study was a case-control study: it starts with the disease and looks back. They interviewed about seven hundred lung cancer patients in twenty London hospitals, each matched with a control, a patient without lung cancer, of the same sex and similar age. Then they compared smoking histories. Nearly every man with lung cancer smoked, and heavy smokers were far more common among the patients than among the controls. To judge any method, use four steps: design, strength, limitation, judgement. The design is case-control. Its strength is speed, and matching made age and sex more comparable. Its limitation is that smoking was remembered, not recorded at the time. That opens the door to bias, a flaw in the method that pushes results one way, which more data can't cancel. The judgement: a strong association, but not yet proof of cause.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Between 1922 and 1947, lung cancer deaths in England and Wales rose about fifteen times. Earlier, you measured disease with rates. Their first study was a case-control study: it starts with the disease and looks back. To judge any method, use four steps: design, strength, limitation, judgement. Critics asked whether a third factor, perhaps something inherited, made people both more likely to smoke and more likely to get lung cancer. Doctors were easy to trace, and their causes of death were well recorded. Now the four steps again. So how did an association become a cause? Several kinds of evidence pointed the same way. Now, what did it achieve? A benefit isn't the finding itself. The benefit was large, mainly because smoking was common and could be changed. Two exam questions. It's case-control: it starts with the disease and looks back. Second. The studies found a risk factor that could be changed. So, for any study.
teaching.openingDecision: Between 1922 and 1947, lung cancer deaths in England and Wales rose about fifteen times. Smoking had grown, but so had tarred roads, car exhaust and factory smoke. In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published the first of their studies on smoking. So how do we judge an epidemiological study, and what it achieved?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. Researchers found three hundred adults with bladder cancer and six hundred without, from the same hospitals, matched for age and sex. Each was asked how often they'd used hair dye over the past twenty years. Evaluate the method used in this study. Pause here to answer. Second. Studies in the 1980s and 90s linked low folate around conception with neural tube defects, where the early brain or spinal cord does not close properly. From 2009, non-organic Australian bread flour had to contain folic acid. Afterwards, neural tube defects fell, most in higher-risk groups. Evaluate the benefit of these studies. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ3-03: "evaluate the method used in an example of an epidemiological study" (scenes 3 to 8, attempt 11a). B8-IQ3-04: "evaluate, using examples, the benefits of engaging in an epidemiological study" (scenes 9 and 10, attempt 11c). Inquiry question: "Why are epidemiological studies used?" (answered in scene 9).

design.visualSystem: One evidence board: a coded study timeline owns the bottom fifth of the frame from scene 2 to scene 8: a horizontal time axis (1948 to 2001) on which each study writes as a coloured span with a direction arrow (the 1950 case-control span points backwards in time from "patients with lung cancer" to "past smoking"; the 1951 cohort span points forwards from "smokers and non-smokers" to "deaths recorded"). Above it, the current study's working: plates, a coded matched-pairs block (case and control dots in pairs), coded record rows (a questionnaire, a ledger line per death), and the coded dose-response chart (house bar chart). A four-slot frame strip ("design → strength → limitation → judgement") writes in scene 4 at the upper right and refills for each study. In scenes 9 and 10, the timeline is replaced by a four-link benefit chain ("finding → decision → action reaches people → outcome checked"), each link a coded box that fills with a small plate or chip. No people, hands or faces: the studies are charts, records, envelopes, ledgers, lungs and airway cells; doctors and patients are coded dots. Researchers are named in narration only, never drawn. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.

scenes.visualReference: the board clears. The card writes on, tagged "HSC-style question, written for HSCScience". Stem: "Epidemiological studies in the 1980s and 1990s found that low folate intake around the time of conception was associated with a higher risk of neural tube defects (the neural tube is the early structure that becomes the brain and spinal cord). The neural tube closes in the first four weeks of pregnancy. From 2009, Australia required non-organic wheat flour for bread-making to contain folic acid. Afterwards, the rate of neural tube defects fell. The largest falls were in the groups with the highest rates before fortification." m6-bread-loaf-crumb-v1.png sits small at the card's upper left. Demand: "Evaluate the benefit of these epidemiological studies. (4 marks)". The countdown ring starts after "Pause here to answer." and runs for 10 seconds. The whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it.
